s: Part one.
Keeping critical information alive.
By the end of this part, you'll know why a long conversation quietly degrades, the four ways to keep the facts that matter, and how to choose between them.
Let's start with the most important fact in the whole domain.
And it surprises people.
The plain version first.
The model does not remember your conversation between turns.
Every time it replies, the entire conversation so far is handed to it again.
Read from the top.
And paid for again.
So the model's working memory behaves less like a cupboard, and more like luggage.
Anything in a cupboard costs you nothing to keep.
Anything in your luggage comes with you on every trip, and you pay for the weight every time.
A bigger suitcase lets you bring more.
It does not make the extra weight free.
And it does not help you find your passport once the bag is stuffed.
That second half matters most.
As the bag fills, the model gets worse at using what is in it.
So a fuller memory is not only more expensive.
Past a certain point, it is less effective.
In exam terms, this is the context window.
The underlying API, the application programming interface, is stateless.
That means nothing persists between calls unless you send it again.
What counts against the window?
Everything.
The system prompt.
Every message.
Every tool result.
Images and documents.
The definitions of the tools themselves.
And the model's output, including extended thinking.
There are two separate limits.
The hard limit is the window size.
Go over it, and you get an error.
The soft limit is more dangerous.
Anthropic's engineering guidance calls it context rot.
As the window fills, attention is stretched across more and more material.
And quality drops silently, while you are still nominally within budget.
A note on numbers, because the exam loves a trap here.
The study notes record that, as of August twenty twenty-six, current models carry a one million token window by default.
Output is capped separately, at one hundred and twenty-eight thousand tokens per request.
And older models, such as Sonnet four point five and Haiku four point five, sit at two hundred thousand.
Those figures move.
Verify them against the current documentation before you design against them.
The principle does not move.
Now the trap.
Two wrong answers appear again and again.
The first is "move to a model with a larger context window."
That raises the ceiling and changes nothing else.
The same degradation comes back, just later in the session.
The self-check in the notes describes exactly this.
A team moves from two hundred thousand tokens to one million.
Six weeks later, the same failure reappears, further into each session.
They treated a density problem as a capacity problem.
The second wrong answer is "raise the maximum output tokens."
That is a separate budget.
It gives the model more room to write.
It does nothing about the noise the model is reading.
Hold on to this line.
The context window is a budget you spend, not a container you fill.
And a bigger one is not a strategy.
So what is the strategy?
The first tool is what I'll call the sticky note.
The plain version.
Go back to our refund agent.
A good human call-centre agent writes three things on a sticky note at the top of her screen.
The confirmed order number.
The refund amount.
And the deadline.
And here's the crucial part.
She copies them from the order system.
Not from what the caller half-remembers.
However long the call runs, she glances at the note.
She doesn't try to recall a figure from twenty minutes ago.
The technical name for this is a case-facts block.
It's a compact block of transactional facts.
Things like the customer ID, the order ID, the refund amount, and the policy-window day.
It's pinned at the top of the context, and rewritten every turn.
It's small.
Typically under a couple of hundred tokens.
And it does two jobs at once.
One.
It removes your dependence on whatever a summary chose to keep.
Two.
It keeps those facts out of the middle of the context, which is where material is used least reliably.
We'll come back to that middle problem in a moment.
Here's how the exam tests it.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
It's our exact refund story.
Forty-five turns.
A customer who said one hundred and fifty-nine ninety-nine.
An order system that said one hundred and forty-nine ninety-nine.
Memory tidied twice.
And the agent quoting the wrong figure back.
There are four options.
Which one fixes it?
Take a second.
The answer.
A facts block, refreshed from tool-confirmed data.
The facts block holds verified tool data only.
Never unverified customer claims.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: a bigger window.
Why?
We've already dismissed it.
It raises the ceiling and nothing else.
Wrong: keep summarising, but instruct the summariser to preserve every amount and date it judges important.
Why?
That still depends on a lossy, model-chosen summary.
The instruction improves the odds.
It guarantees nothing.
Wrong: a facts block refreshed from each customer message.
Why?
This one is the near miss.
It looks almost identical to the right answer.
Right structure, wrong source.
If you pin what the customer said, you pin the wrong one hundred and fifty-nine ninety-nine.
The stem word that decides it is the moment the tool corrected the customer.
When you hear that, think verified-only facts.
Takeaway.
Pin the facts at the top, and pin only what a tool has confirmed.
The second tool is trimming.
It's about the biggest, noisiest thing in the window: tool output.
The plain version.
A clerk gets a forty-page delivery report every morning.
She needs only four lines of it.
If she stacks every full report on her desk, within a week she can't find anything.
So she copies the four lines onto an index card.
She files the report in a cabinet.
And she writes the drawer number on the card.
Nothing is lost.
It's just not on the desk.
In exam terms, you trim tool output before it accumulates, at the hook layer.
In Claude Code, a hook is a small script the system runs automatically at a set point.
A PostToolUse hook runs right after a tool returns.
And it can replace what the model sees with a trimmed version.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
A continuous integration job, CI for short.
Each test-runner call returns about twenty thousand tokens of log.
The agent needs only failing test names, file paths, line numbers and assertion messages.
After five or six calls, the agent starts blaming the wrong files.
And one more constraint: "the full logs must remain available for later audit."
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
A post-tool hook that keeps only the failing test identifiers, paths and messages.
And it saves each raw log as a file, referenced by its path.
About sixty tokens reach the context, instead of twenty thousand.
The study notes show the same move on a server diagnostic.
A roughly nine-hundred-token dump, reduced to a sixty-token finding.
It keeps the exact names, the numbers, the open question.
And one last line pointing at the raw output on disk.
That last line is the difference between trimming and destroying.
Now the wrong turns.
And this trap is subtle, because the wrong answers are real platform features.
Wrong: server-side tool-result clearing.
Why?
Clearing removes old tool results outright once a token threshold is passed.
So an identifier that lived only in a cleared log is not blurred.
It's gone.
And nothing points back to it.
Wrong: server-side compaction.
Why?
Compaction summarises the accumulated history into a short narrative.
That's lossy and model-written.
And file paths and test identifiers are exactly the details that degrade first.
Notice that both of those act after the bloat.
The hook acts before it.
And the constraint word that seals it is "the full logs must remain available for later audit."
When a stem says auditable later, think raw-output path.
Takeaway.
Trim before it piles up, and always keep a path back to the original.
Those two features just appeared as distractors.
So let's name them properly.
This is a genuine contrast segment, because the exam checks whether you can tell them apart.
The plain version.
Think of the luggage again.
There are three moves.
Compaction is repacking.
You swap the bulky originals for a short written note of what they contained.
And you accept that a note is not the thing.
Context editing is lifting named items out of the bag.
More precise, because you say what goes.
But what goes is gone.
Writing facts to disk is checking a bag through.
It costs nothing to carry, and one errand to retrieve.
Now the technical version.
One caveat first.
These identifiers come from the study notes, and they were in beta when the notes were written.
So check current documentation.
Server-side compaction is identified as compact_20260112.
Here's what it does.
It watches input tokens against a trigger.
It generates a summary.
It returns a compaction block.
And on later requests, the API drops everything before that block.
The notes say the trigger defaults to one hundred and fifty thousand input tokens, and cannot go below fifty thousand.
The default summary asks for four things.
Conversation state.
Next steps.
Learnings.
And decisions.
There's an option called instructions.
And here's the catch.
It replaces the default summarisation prompt entirely.
It doesn't add to it.
So anything you still want from the default has to be restated.
Context editing is the surgical pair.
It uses a strategy called clear_tool_uses_20250919, to drop the oldest tool results past a threshold.
And a strategy called clear_thinking_20251015, to manage thinking blocks.
When you use both, the clear_thinking_20251015 edit must come first in the list of edits.
The notes add that context editing is switched on with a beta header: context-management-2025-06-27.
All of these run server-side, before the prompt reaches the model.
So your own client still holds the full, unmodified history.
Now the trap.
When compaction damages identifiers, three tempting fixes appear.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A regulatory agent invented a rule identifier after compaction.
What's the right fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Write each identifier to a durable record at the moment it is discovered.
And have the agent read identifiers from that record, not from conversation history.
Two more things help.
You can tell compaction's instructions to reproduce identifiers verbatim.
And you can use a PreCompact hook, which fires before compaction, to archive the transcript.
Both help.
But the persisted record is the stronger guarantee.
Why?
Because it doesn't depend on a model following an instruction.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: raise the compaction trigger, so it fires less often.
Why?
That delays the failure rather than preventing it.
A long-lived session crosses any trigger eventually.
Wrong: disable compaction.
Why?
On a long-lived session, that leads to a hard overflow.
And warnings about remaining budget preserve nothing.
Wrong: swap compaction for clearing, because clearing doesn't rewrite anything.
Why?
That's true, but clearing deletes.
An identifier that lived only in a cleared result is simply gone.
That's at least as bad.
Hold on to this line.
Extract before you clear.
Persist before you summarise.
Identifiers, exact figures, file paths and line numbers are never summarisable.
Now the middle problem I promised.
The plain version.
Hand someone a thick stack of papers, with one crucial instruction buried on page two hundred.
They're more likely to miss it than if it sat on the first page or the last.
The top and the bottom of the pile are where things get found.
In exam terms, here's what Anthropic's prompting guidance says.
Put long documents and bulk inputs near the top of the prompt, above the query and instructions.
It reports that putting the question at the end can improve response quality by up to thirty percent in tests.
Especially with complex multi-document inputs.
This lines up with a research finding called "lost in the middle."
Material near the start or end of a long input is used most reliably.
Material in the middle, least.
Treat that as a tendency, not a law.
It was measured on particular tasks and models, and modern models handle it better.
So the practical layout has three layers.
Facts at the top.
Trimmed results in the middle.
And last, a one-line recap of constraints, plus the question.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
A practice question puts one hard constraint in the middle of a three-hundred-and-eighty-thousand-token document set.
The constraint is: never report on entities incorporated outside the European Union.
What's the best answer?
Take a second.
The answer has three pieces.
It names the position effect.
It moves documents first and instructions last.
And it also validates the constraint outside the model.
That last clause matters.
Placement improves the odds.
It never makes a hard constraint reliable.
This connects to the enforcement ladder from earlier chapters.
Anything that must happen every time belongs in code.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: the input exceeds the usable window and should be split.
Why?
Splitting breaks the cross-document reasoning.
Wrong: anything outside the system prompt is ignored.
Why?
That overstates it.
Wrong: blame vague wording, "regardless of where it sits."
Why?
That contradicts the placement guidance.
And watch for one more reversal.
Wrong: an option that moves the bulk material after the question.
Why?
That's backwards.
Takeaway.
Bulk material first, the question last, and hard constraints checked in code as well.
The last concept in this part is choosing among the preservation strategies.
And it's where the exam likes a phase change.
The plain version.
You've just had a long brainstorming meeting, and half the ideas were rejected.
You don't hand the builder the full recording.
You give them a one-page work order.
What was decided.
What was ruled out.
And the exact addresses they need.
Whatever is not on the page will not reach them.
So you write it carefully.
The technical version is a four-way choice.
Let's take them one at a time.
One.
Trim in place.
Use it when the output is bulky and low density, and the facts are easy to list.
It has the lowest ongoing cost.
The risk is losing an identifier you didn't know you needed.
Two.
Summarise, through compaction or your own summary turn.
Use it when the reasoning path matters more than the raw artifacts.
The risk is that it's lossy and model-chosen.
Three.
Persist to disk and reload on demand.
Use it for anything that must survive word for word.
The cost is a little latency.
The risk is stale files.
Four.
Start a fresh session with a handoff brief.
Use it when the task has changed phase, or when the history is more contradiction than context.
It has the highest one-off authoring cost, and the cheapest steady state.
And its risk is total.
Anything not in the brief is gone.
The notes' honest reading is this.
Persist-to-disk is the default for facts.
Compaction is the default for narrative.
And they combine well.
Anthropic's guidance calls that pairing structured note-taking alongside compaction.
Quick recap before the last question.
Trim bulk.
Summarise narrative.
Persist facts.
And start fresh when the task has changed phase.
Question five.
Here's the scenario.
Four hours in one Claude Code session, investigating a flaky build.
The investigation is done.
The work has moved to implementing a fix.
The history is full of abandoned hypotheses.
And the agent keeps reverting to an approach the developer ruled out two hours ago.
What's the best move?
Take a second.
The answer.
A fresh session, with a handoff brief.
The brief carries the two locked decisions, the ruled-out approach, and the exact file paths.
And one detail.
Findings from the old session that are not yet confirmed go in as hypotheses to validate.
Not as facts.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: add a strongly worded reminder.
Why?
It's one more sentence competing with hours of contradiction.
And it's the first thing lost.
Wrong: trigger compaction.
Why?
Compaction suits a session where the reasoning path matters.
But here the path is mostly abandoned ideas.
A model-chosen summary may keep them, and blur the paths.
Wrong: a bigger window.
Why?
It keeps all the contradiction in view.
The stem words that flip the answer are "the work has moved on" and "keeps reverting."
Phase change, plus contradictory history, means a fresh brief.
So when do you compact, and when do you start fresh?
Compact when the journey is the value, and you're continuing the same task.
Start fresh when the journey is mostly wrong turns, and the task has changed.
In both cases, write the must-survive facts down first.
That's part one.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Trim bulk, summarise narrative, persist facts, and start fresh with a careful brief when the history has turned against you.

When to fetch a human, and what to do when a request is unclear.
